Kestrel Bay crews switch to quieter nets

A small trial could change how the bay’s fleet fishes for good.

KESTREL BAY
Fishing crews here have started testing a new kind of net that uses lighter mesh and small acoustic pingers, in an attempt to keep porpoises and seabirds away from their catch. Six boats joined the trial in September, and four more are expected to sign up before winter.

The nets were designed by a marine lab in the north, which spent two years adjusting the pinger tones so that they warn off porpoises without scaring the fish. Early results suggest that bycatch has fallen by about half on the trial boats, although the sample is still small.

Skipper Joan Pell, who has fished the bay for thirty-one years, said she was sceptical at first. “I thought it would cost us half our catch,” she said. “So far it’s cost us almost nothing, and the boat is quieter, which my crew likes.”

The nets are more expensive than the old ones, at roughly twice the price, and the batteries in the pingers need replacing every few weeks. A regional fund is covering the cost for the trial boats, but crews worry about what will happen when the funding ends in 2028.

Conservation groups have welcomed the trial, while pointing out that the bay’s porpoise population is still falling. They want the regional council to make the nets compulsory, a step the council has said it will consider only after the full results are published next year.
